title: Cheyenne County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Cheyenne County wells have a median depth of 76 ft and a median yield of 15 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost and water supply on your land.
h1: Water wells in Cheyenne County, Colorado
intro_html:
Cheyenne County is classic eastern Colorado plains: mostly stock and irrigation wells, with a fair number of domestic wells for homes and farmsteads. The state has 2,092 well permits on record here, and over a thousand of those report depth and yield, so we have a decent picture of what to expect.

If you are looking at land around Cheyenne Wells, Arapahoe, or Kit Carson, the numbers below give you a realistic idea of how deep a new well may need to go, how much water it is likely to produce, and what a drilling bid might look like under local conditions.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Cheyenne County
sections.html:
Across Cheyenne County, the median well depth is 76 feet, but there is a wide spread. The middle half of wells run from 34 to 256 feet, and the deepest on record goes down to 630 feet. About 52% of wells are under 100 feet, 30% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 18% are between 300 and 600 feet.

That mix tells you a driller can hit water shallow in some areas, but in others you may have to chase it several hundred feet, especially in the fractured-bedrock settings that make up 1,530 of the permitted wells. Ogallala wells (404 recorded) also factor in, especially for irrigation. Any bid here should allow for the possibility of going well past the 76-foot median.

sections.heading: Well yields and how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Cheyenne County wells are generally decent producers for plains country. The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 27.8 gpm. No wells in the records show under 1 gpm, 10% fall in the 1–5 gpm range, 32% are 5–15 gpm, and 57% report 15 gpm or higher.

For a single-family exempt domestic well, anything over 1–2 gpm is usually workable with storage, so these county-wide numbers are reassuring. Stock and irrigation uses, which make up 50% and 23% of permits, lean on the stronger Ogallala and better bedrock wells. Still, there is a meaningful 1–5 gpm slice, so it is smart to look closely at nearby well yields before closing on a parcel, especially outside the main developed areas.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend on the plains
sections.html:
Static water levels in Cheyenne County average a bit deeper than well depth might suggest. The overall median depth to water is 89 feet, with the middle half between 26 and 182 feet below ground surface. That means some wells have water standing not too far below the surface, while others are drawing from relatively deep.

By decade, median water levels have bounced around: about 132 feet in the 1960s, 164 in the 1970s, then shallower at 40 feet in the 2010s and around 93 feet in the 2020s. That pattern looks more like variable conditions and changing measurement locations than a steady drop or rise. In short, there is no clear long-term decline signal in the county-wide numbers, but your actual water level will depend heavily on whether you are in Ogallala, alluvium, or fractured bedrock.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling and when around here
sections.html:
Cheyenne County has a long history of well development. Permit activity picked up in the 1970s with 241 permits, stayed strong with 175 in the 1980s and 232 in the 1990s, and peaked in the 2000s at 249. The 2010s saw 156 permits, and there are already 89 in the 2020s, with records running through 2025.

Most wells are for stock (50%) and irrigation (23%), with domestic and household use accounting for 21% and monitoring wells 8%. The main drillers on record are Kemp'S Well Service (367 wells), Schaal Drilling Co. (87), and Eastwood Drilling (79). When you see these names on nearby well logs, it is a sign the driller knows local formations and can give more accurate expectations for depth and yield in your immediate area.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Cheyenne County
sections.html:
Here, the ground is mostly alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, which tends to drill at a moderate rate. The typical local price runs about $35–$55 per foot. At the county-wide median depth of 76 feet, that puts just the drilled hole in the ballpark of $2,700–$4,200.

Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching to the house, and electrical work, a completed domestic well around that depth often lands roughly in the $8,700–$16,200 range. If you end up closer to the upper middle depths, say around 200 feet instead of the 76-foot median, you are proportionally increasing the drilling portion of the bill, so it is smart to budget assuming you might need to go into the 100–300 foot range that covers 30% of local wells.

sections.heading: Key risks to check: water quality, low yield, and siting
sections.html:
Most Cheyenne County wells perform adequately, but you still want to think through risk. There are 59 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, so testing any existing well for a full contaminant panel, not just bacteria, is important.

While there are no recorded wells under 1 gpm, about 10% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. That is livable for a home with storage, but it is marginal for heavy irrigation or large livestock numbers. Also pay attention to septic layout and building locations: make sure there is room to keep the well uphill and away from leach fields and corrals. In fractured bedrock in particular, yields can be hit-or-miss from one spot to the next even on the same parcel.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Cheyenne County
sections.html:
Before you buy land outside Cheyenne Wells, Arapahoe, or Kit Carson, pull the nearby well permits from the state and look at three things: depth, yield, and aquifer. Around here, most wells are in unnamed fractured bedrock, with 404 tapping the Ogallala and a handful in alluvium. Those details can change your risk profile considerably.

If the parcel has no well, assume you might need more than the 76-foot median and budget toward the 34–256 foot middle range, especially for stock or irrigation uses. Check that your intended house and septic locations leave proper setbacks from a future well. Finally, in areas flagged for PFAS or other cleanup activity, plan on upfront water testing and possibly filtration as part of your build cost.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Cheyenne County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Cheyenne County, the median well depth is 76 feet. The middle half of wells fall between 34 and 256 feet, and about 18% run between 300 and 600 feet. No wells are recorded deeper than 630 feet. Just over half of the wells are under 100 feet, but a substantial share still need 100–300 feet of drilling, so depth can vary a lot by location.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Cheyenne County, CO?
faq.a: Reported yields in Cheyenne County are generally solid for domestic and stock use. The median yield is 15.0 gpm, with the middle half of wells between 10.0 and 27.8 gpm. About 57% of wells report 15 gpm or more, 32% are in the 5–15 gpm range, and 10% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. There are no wells recorded under 1 gpm in the available data.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Cheyenne County, Colorado?
faq.a: With local alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, typical drilling runs about $35–$55 per foot in Cheyenne County. At the median well depth of 76 feet, the drilled hole alone is roughly $2,700–$4,200. A complete domestic setup with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually ends up in the $8,700–$16,200 range, with deeper wells costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Cheyenne County, CO?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Cheyenne County has 59 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, so testing is important. Before relying on a well for drinking, have it checked for bacteria, nitrates, and a broader contaminant panel where PFAS or other industrial impacts are possible. Treatment is available if tests show problems.

faq.q: Are water tables dropping in Cheyenne County, Colorado?
faq.a: County-wide static water level data do not show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was about 132 feet in the 1960s, 164 feet in the 1970s, then much shallower at 40 feet in the 2010s and around 93 feet in the 2020s. Overall, the median today is 89 feet with a wide 26–182 foot middle range. That suggests variability by area and aquifer more than one uniform trend.
